name: Protestant / Anglican
blurb: A marriage service in church with hymns, vows and the signing of the schedule, whether that is a Church of England parish wedding after banns or a Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian or Lutheran service shaped by your own congregation.

events.name: Meetings with the vicar or minister
events.description: Every tradition expects at least one unhurried conversation before the wedding, and most expect several. A Church of England vicar will talk through the service, the legal preliminaries and what marriage means; many parishes also run short marriage preparation sessions. In the US, Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian and Lutheran pastors commonly ask for a series of premarital counselling meetings before they agree to officiate.

events.name: Reading of the banns
events.when: Three Sundays in the three months before
events.description: Church of England weddings in England and Wales are usually preceded by banns: your intention to marry is announced at the main Sunday service on three Sundays in the church where you will marry and in the parish where each of you lives. Many couples go along to hear their own banns read and are prayed for by the congregation. Other denominations and other countries do not use banns; a register office notice or state licence takes their place.

events.name: Hen and stag celebrations
events.description: A hen and stag do in Britain and Ireland, a bachelorette and bachelor party in the US. Organised and usually paid for by the wedding party rather than the couple. Nothing about them is religious, so shape them however suits you.

events.name: Rehearsal and rehearsal dinner
events.when: The evening before, or a few days before
events.description: The vicar or minister walks the wedding party, readers and musicians through the service, usually in the week before the wedding. The rehearsal dinner afterwards is a well-established American custom, traditionally hosted by the groom's family; in Britain the rehearsal is more often followed by nothing grander than the pub.
events.hosts: Traditionally the groom's family in the US

events.name: The marriage service
events.description: Typically 30 to 45 minutes: entrance, a hymn, a statement of what marriage is, the declarations, readings and a short address, the vows, the giving of rings, the proclamation that you are married, prayers and the signing of the marriage schedule or licence. Anglican, Methodist, Presbyterian and Lutheran services follow a set liturgy with room for choices; Baptist and other free-church services are shaped by the pastor and can feel closer to a service built around you. Holy Communion can be included in Anglican, Methodist and Lutheran weddings but most couples keep the service without it.

events.name: Photographs and confetti at the church door
events.description: Group photographs outside the church, often with bells ringing, followed by a confetti send-off as you leave. Check what the church allows to be thrown and where; many ask for biodegradable petals outside the gate.

events.name: Drinks reception
events.when: Wedding day, between church and meal
events.description: Drinks and canapés while photographs are finished and guests travel from the church to the reception venue. Usually an hour to ninety minutes. If your reception is in a church hall, check the rules on alcohol first, because many Methodist and Baptist premises are alcohol-free.

events.name: Wedding breakfast and speeches
events.description: The main meal, known in Britain as the wedding breakfast whatever the hour. Speeches traditionally come from the father of the bride, the groom and the best man, with toasts after each, though many couples now add or substitute other voices. Grace is often said before the meal, sometimes by the vicar or minister if invited.
events.hosts: Traditionally the bride's family; now commonly shared or paid by the couple

events.name: Evening reception
events.description: In Britain a second wave of evening guests often arrives for the cake cutting, first dance, band or DJ and evening food. In the US the reception more commonly runs as one continuous event for a single guest list.

events.name: Day-after gathering
events.description: A relaxed brunch or lunch for family and guests who have travelled, common in the US as a morning-after brunch and increasingly seen in Britain. Entirely optional and usually informal.
events.hosts: Often the parents or the couple

items.name: Church wedding fee
items.note: In the Church of England the marriage service has a statutory fee set nationally each year, the same in every parish. It covers the vicar, the church, calling your banns, a banns certificate, lighting and administration; it is a little higher if one or both of you live outside the parish, because banns must also be called there. Other denominations set their own charges: a Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian or Lutheran congregation will usually quote a building fee plus staffing, and many reduce or waive it for members. Ask for an itemised written quote so you can see what is included.

items.name: Banns, licence or notice fees
items.note: The legal preliminaries. For a Church of England wedding, banns are included in the statutory fee, but a common licence, used when banns are not possible, costs noticeably more and involves swearing an oath in person before a legal official. For other denominations in England and Wales, each of you gives notice at a register office and pays the notice fee. In Scotland each of you lodges a marriage notice with the registrar; in the US the marriage licence fee is paid to the county or state.

items.name: Registrar attendance
items.note: A Church of England wedding never needs a registrar, because the clergy themselves have legal authority. Other denominations in England and Wales marry in a registered building with an authorised person, often the minister or a church officer; if your chapel has none, you must book a registrar to attend, at a fee set by the local council, and their diaries fill up for summer Saturdays. Not applicable in Scotland or the US, where the minister acts alone.

items.name: Gift or honorarium for a visiting minister
items.note: If your own vicar or minister marries you, their part is covered by the church fee in the Church of England and by the congregation's quote elsewhere. A minister who travels from another church, a family friend who officiates, or a US pastor is customarily given an honorarium, and travel and accommodation if they have come some distance. There is rarely a stated figure; ask the church office what is usual.

items.name: Marriage preparation or premarital counselling
items.note: Not a legal requirement anywhere, but many churches ask for it. Church of England parishes often run free or low-cost preparation days; US pastors across the mainline denominations commonly require a short course or a series of counselling sessions, sometimes with a workbook or inventory fee. A few US states reduce the marriage licence fee for couples who complete an approved course.

items.name: Organist
items.note: The organist plays the processional, accompanies the hymns, covers the signing and plays you out. Fees are set locally by the church, and organists routinely charge more if the wedding is filmed, because recording engages performance rights. Book through the church rather than around it; most churches expect you to use their own organist or to seek permission for a substitute.

items.name: Church choir
items.note: A choir lifts the hymns and can sing an anthem during the signing. Charged per head or as a set fee at the church's local rate, with the same filming surcharge as the organist. In churches without a regular choir, a small professional ensemble can usually be brought in with the minister's agreement.

items.name: Bell ringers
items.note: A peal of bells as you leave is one of the sounds of an English church wedding, where the tower has bells and a band to ring them. Charged at the church's local rate. Largely a Church of England and older-parish feature; most Methodist, Baptist and newer churches do not have a ring of bells.

items.name: Verger or caretaker
items.note: Prepares the church, helps seat guests and manages access on the day. An optional extra at the church's local rate in the Church of England; elsewhere the equivalent may appear on the quote as a caretaker or facilities fee.

items.name: Church heating
items.note: A real line for autumn and winter weddings in older buildings, charged where the church needs to run extra heating for the service. Ask when you book rather than discovering it on the invoice.

items.name: Reception venue hire
items.note: Hotel, barn, hall or marquee. Because the church is fixed and the reception is not, factor in the journey between the two. Church halls can be good value but often carry conditions: Methodist premises are alcohol-free as a rule of the denomination, and many Baptist churches are similar, so check before you plan a bar.

items.name: Wedding breakfast
items.note: Usually the single largest line. Check whether the per-head price includes service, VAT or sales tax, corkage and cake cutting, and whether suppliers such as the photographer and band are fed. Nothing about the meal is religious, so let the venue and your budget lead.

items.name: Bar, wine and toast drink
items.note: Reception drinks, table wine and something for the toasts. Plan around your venue's rules: hotels usually insist on supplying drink themselves, halls may let you run your own bar, and church premises may not allow alcohol at all, in which case a good non-alcoholic toast is entirely normal in Methodist and Baptist circles.

items.name: Evening food
items.note: In Britain the evening guest list is often larger than the daytime one, and evening food, a hog roast, bacon rolls or a buffet, is costed separately. Less of a distinct line in the US, where one guest list usually runs through the whole reception.

items.name: Wedding cake
items.note: The cake cutting is usually the signal that the evening has begun. Traditional British wedding cake is rich fruit cake, with the top tier kept for a christening or first anniversary; sponge tiers now outsell fruit almost everywhere. Check whether the venue charges a cutting fee.

items.name: Rehearsal dinner
items.note: An American custom, traditionally hosted by the groom's family for the wedding party, immediate family and out-of-town guests. Rare in Britain, where the money more often goes into the evening reception instead. Turn it on only if your families expect it.

items.name: Day-after brunch
items.note: A simple gathering the day after for family and travelling guests. Usually informal, often at home or in a pub or restaurant, and one of the easiest lines to trim.

items.name: Wedding dress and alterations
items.note: Most Protestant churches have no dress code for the bride, and shoulders do not need to be covered. Allow a long lead time for ordering plus two or three fittings. If the church has a long aisle and you want a train and veil, tell the photographer and whoever is managing the entrance.

items.name: Veil, shoes and accessories
items.note: Veil, shoes, jewellery and whatever carries the something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue if you keep that custom. None of it is required by the church.

items.name: Groom's outfit
items.note: Morning dress remains common at formal English church weddings, lounge suits everywhere else, and a hired kilt outfit is standard at many Scottish weddings. Hiring for the groom and groomsmen together usually brings the per-head price down.

items.name: Wedding party outfits
items.note: Bridesmaids, groomsmen, flower girls and page boys. Who pays varies by family and country: in Britain the couple more often buy the bridesmaids' dresses, in the US attendants commonly buy their own. Decide early and say so plainly.

items.name: Hair and make-up
items.note: Trial plus the wedding morning. Work backwards from the service time; church weddings often start earlier in the day than civil ones, and the church books its slot around other services.

items.name: Wedding party hair and make-up
items.note: Bridesmaids and mothers, priced per head. The line that quietly grows once the morning schedule is drawn up, so fix numbers before you fix the price.

items.name: Church flowers
items.note: Pedestal arrangements, windowsills and pew ends. Many churches have a flower team who will arrange for a donation, which is often better value than bringing a florist in. Some churches keep the building bare or restrained during Lent and Advent, and at Christmas and Easter it will already be decorated, so ask what will be in place for your date. If another wedding shares your weekend, sharing flowers and cost is common sense.

items.name: Bouquets and buttonholes
items.note: Bridal bouquet, bridesmaids' flowers, buttonholes for the groom's side and corsages for mothers. If you plan to toss the bouquet and also keep it, ask the florist for a small throwing copy.

items.name: Reception flowers and styling
items.note: Centrepieces, top table and any larger styling. Church arrangements can often move to the reception afterwards if someone is tasked with carrying them, which stretches the same flowers across the whole day.

items.name: Lighting and decor
items.note: Uplighting, festoons and dance-floor lighting. More relevant for halls, barns and marquees than for hotels, which usually come dressed.

items.name: Photographer
items.note: Photography in church is at the discretion of the vicar or minister. Most allow discreet photography and many are relaxed, but some restrict movement or flash during the vows, and a few allow photographs only at the entrance and the signing. Ask what your church permits and pass it to the photographer in writing before the day.

items.name: Videographer
items.note: Needs the same church permission as photography, and filming has a knock-on cost: organists and choirs usually charge a higher fee when the service is recorded, because of performance rights in the music. Budget for that supplement, not just the videographer.

items.name: Band or DJ
items.note: The evening's main entertainment, opening with the first dance. Entirely a cultural choice with no church involvement, though if the reception is on church premises, check for any conditions on amplified music and finish times. A ceilidh band is a popular choice at Scottish and northern English weddings.

items.name: Daytime musicians
items.note: A string quartet, harpist or acoustic act for the drinks reception, or a piper at a Scottish wedding to play the couple out of the church and into the reception. If you want them to play inside the church as well, clear the repertoire with the vicar or minister.

items.name: Invitations and save the dates
items.note: Traditional wording names the hosts, historically the bride's parents, and invites guests to the marriage service at the church followed by the reception. If you have separate daytime and evening guest lists, order two versions and keep careful track of who gets which.

items.name: Order of service booklets
items.note: Carries the hymns with full words, the readings and the shape of the service so guests can join in; congregational singing works far better when everyone has the words. Have the vicar or minister check the draft before printing, both for accuracy and because hymn texts still in copyright need a licence to reproduce, which the church usually holds.

items.name: On-the-day stationery
items.note: Table plan, place cards, menus and signage for the reception.

items.name: Wedding cars
items.note: Bride and bridesmaids to the church, couple to the reception. Ask about parking and turning space at the church gate; village churches in particular can be tight, and the vicar will know what works.

items.name: Guest transport
items.note: A coach between church and reception is worth costing whenever the two are far apart, which is common because the church is fixed by parish or congregation and the reception is not.

items.name: Wedding rings
items.note: The giving of rings sits at the centre of the service in every tradition covered here, with words spoken over each ring as it is given. One ring or two is your choice. Give them to the best man before the service; producing them at the right moment is his one non-negotiable duty.

items.name: Gifts for the wedding party and parents
items.note: Thank-you gifts for attendants, parents, readers and anyone who has taken on real work. Traditionally mentioned in the groom's speech as each is thanked.

items.name: Favours
items.note: A small gift at each place setting. Entirely optional, no religious meaning, and one of the easiest lines to cut without anyone noticing.

items.name: Wedding night and guest accommodation
items.note: Your own room, and often rooms held for parents and travelling family. If the church and reception are in a rural spot, block-booking nearby rooms early saves guests a scramble.

items.name: Wedding insurance
items.note: Covers supplier failure, cancellation and damage. Some venues and marquee firms require public liability cover as a condition of booking, so check before you decline it.

timeline.task: Contact the church before booking anything else, and ask about dates, fees and what the church expects of you

If either of you has been married before, raise it at the first conversation: remarriage is at the discretion of the individual vicar or minister in most Protestant churches

Draft the guest list, decide daytime versus evening guests, and agree with both families who is paying for what
Book the photographer and videographer, and ask the vicar or minister what photography is allowed during the service
Book the band or DJ for the evening
Start dress shopping, allowing for order lead time plus alterations
Book the florist, and ask whether the church has its own flower team and any seasonal restrictions
Send save the dates, particularly if guests are travelling
Begin marriage preparation or premarital counselling if your church runs or requires it, which most US pastors do
Choose hymns, readings and the form of vows with the vicar or minister, and decide whether to include Holy Communion
Book the organist, and the choir and bell ringers if you want them, telling them now if the service will be filmed
Order invitations

Confirm your legal route: banns for most Church of England weddings, a common or special licence where banns will not work, register office notice for other denominations in England and Wales, marriage notice in Scotland, or a state licence in the US

If either of you is not a British or Irish citizen without settled status, tell the vicar now, because the wedding will need a superintendent registrar's schedule instead of banns and notice can take longer
Church of England: arrange banns at the wedding church and at the parish church where each of you lives

Send invitations

paperwork.note: The standard preliminary for Church of England weddings in England and Wales. Your intention to marry is published on three Sundays, not necessarily consecutive, at the main service in the church where you will marry and in the parish where each of you lives. The wedding must then take place within three months of the last reading.

paperwork.item: Banns certificate from your home parish
paperwork.who: Each of you living outside the wedding parish
paperwork.note: Proof that banns were read in your own parish, issued by that church and handed to the wedding church before the day. Easy to forget and impossible to do without.

paperwork.who: Both, if banns will not work
paperwork.note: The Church of England alternative when there is not enough time for banns, when one of you lives outside England and Wales, or when an address will change during the banns period. Granted at the discretion of the diocesan legal official, it requires one of you to swear an oath in person, names a specific church, and is valid for three months.

Granted by the Archbishop of Canterbury's Faculty Office for marriages that cannot happen under the normal rules, most often in a school or college chapel or a church where neither of you has a qualifying connection. Not quick and never automatic.

Required instead of banns for a Church of England wedding when either of you is not a British or Irish citizen and lacks EU settled status. Notice is given at the register office and published for 28 days, which can be extended to 70 for immigration checks.

paperwork.item: Notice of marriage at the register office
paperwork.who: Both, for non-Anglican church weddings in England and Wales
paperwork.note: Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Lutheran and other chapels are registered buildings, so each of you gives notice in your registration district at least 29 days before the wedding. Notice is valid for twelve months and names the building, so a change of venue means giving notice again. The building normally needs to be in a district where one of you lives, unless it is your usual place of worship.

A non-Anglican wedding in England and Wales needs either the building's authorised person, often the minister, or a registrar booked to attend. Confirm early which applies to your chapel; if a registrar is needed, their availability can constrain your date.

If you are marrying in a parish where neither of you lives, bring evidence of the connection: old utility bills or the electoral roll for past residence, a baptism entry, the worship register, or a parent's or grandparent's marriage entry in that church.

paperwork.item: Passport or photo identification and proof of address
paperwork.note: Needed for banns and licence applications, register office notice, and marriage licence applications in the US.

paperwork.item: Decree absolute, or former spouse's death certificate
paperwork.note: The legal document is only the start in church terms. In the Church of England, marrying again while a former spouse is living has been possible since 2002 but rests with the individual vicar, who will want a frank conversation first; some clergy will instead offer a service of prayer and dedication after a register office wedding. Methodist, Church of Scotland, and most Presbyterian, Lutheran and Baptist ministers may remarry divorced people, but each minister decides, and conservative congregations may decline.

paperwork.item: Marriage schedule or marriage document signed on the day
paperwork.note: In England and Wales couples no longer sign a register book in church; you, two witnesses and the officiant sign a schedule or marriage document during the service, the church or registrar returns it to the register office, and the marriage certificate is issued by the register office afterwards rather than handed over on the day. Order certified copies for name changes.

Each of you lodges a marriage notice with the registrar for the district of the wedding, no later than 29 days and no earlier than three months before. The schedule is collected in person no more than seven days before the ceremony, signed on the day by you, two witnesses and the minister, and returned to the registrar within three days. Because Scots law authorises the celebrant rather than the building, a Church of Scotland minister can marry you anywhere in Scotland.

Issued by the county clerk or equivalent, usually on proof of identity and payment of a fee. Validity commonly runs 30 to 90 days and a few states impose a short waiting period, so collect it in the window your state allows. The officiant completes and returns it after the ceremony.

Ordained ministers of these denominations are recognised in every state, but a few places add local rules, such as New York City's requirement for officiants to register with the city clerk. A minister travelling from another state or country should check well ahead.

The Church of England marries residents of the parish whether or not they attend church, and asks for no baptism certificate from the couple. Baptist and some other free churches, especially in the US, may expect one or both of you to be members, to be baptised believers, or to complete counselling before the pastor agrees. Ask at the first meeting rather than assuming.

customs.name: Hearing your banns read
customs.description: Couples marrying in the Church of England often attend the Sunday services where their banns are read, are welcomed by name and prayed for by the congregation. A quiet, old custom that many couples find unexpectedly moving.

customs.name: Something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue
customs.description: The Victorian rhyme for what a bride carries on the day. Folk custom rather than anything the church asks for, and cheerfully optional.

customs.name: Walking down the aisle
customs.description: The bride traditionally enters last, on her father's arm, to a processional played on the organ. Modern services are flexible: entering with both parents, with children, alone, or together as a couple are all accepted, and the clergy will not blink.

customs.name: Giving away
customs.description: The moment the bride's father, or another family member, gives her hand to the groom. It is optional in modern Anglican and most Protestant services, and many couples replace it with a question to both families or drop it entirely.

customs.name: Congregational hymns
customs.description: Two or three hymns sung by everyone are the backbone of a Protestant wedding. Perennial choices in Britain include Love Divine, All Loves Excelling, Guide Me, O Thou Great Redeemer, Give Me Joy in My Heart and Jerusalem. Print the full words in the order of service and pick at least one tune people actually know.

customs.name: Organ processional and recessional
customs.description: Wagner's Bridal Chorus in and Mendelssohn's Wedding March out are the classic pairing, with Pachelbel's Canon and Widor's Toccata close behind. Most Protestant churches are relaxed about these and about other classical choices; discuss anything unusual with the organist.

customs.name: The vows
customs.description: The familiar English vows, for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, till death us do part, descend from the Book of Common Prayer and are shared, with small variations, across the Protestant world. In the Church of England the couple choose between traditional and modern language, and the bride may choose whether or not to say obey. In many US churches, particularly Baptist, couples may also write personal vows alongside or around the traditional ones.

customs.name: The declarations
customs.description: Before the vows, each of you answers I will to the questions establishing that you come freely. In Methodist, Presbyterian and Lutheran services the families and congregation are often asked to promise their support out loud as well.

customs.name: Exchange of rings
customs.description: One ring or two, given with words of promise. The best man traditionally keeps the rings and produces them at the right moment.

customs.name: Signing the schedule
customs.description: The couple, two witnesses and the officiant sign the marriage schedule or licence during or immediately after the service, usually while the choir sings or the organist plays. Photographers are almost always allowed a posed shot of the signing.

customs.name: Church bells
customs.description: Where the tower has bells, a peal rung as the couple leave is one of the great sounds of an English parish wedding. Book the ringers early; a full band is not always available.

customs.name: Confetti at the church door
customs.description: Guests shower the couple as they leave the church. Most churches now ask for biodegradable petals or rice alternatives and some restrict where it can be thrown, so check and tell your guests.

customs.name: The receiving line
customs.description: The couple and both sets of parents greet every guest on arrival at the reception. Falling out of fashion because of the time it takes, but older relatives often expect it.

customs.name: Wedding breakfast and speeches
customs.description: The British order of speeches is father of the bride, then the groom, then the best man, each ending in a toast; the best man traditionally reads messages from absent friends. American receptions typically have shorter toasts from the best man and maid of honour instead.

customs.name: Cutting the cake
customs.description: The couple make the first cut together, traditionally as the first act of their marriage and now usually the signal that the dancing is about to start. The top tier of a fruit cake is traditionally kept for a christening or first anniversary.

customs.name: First dance
customs.description: The couple open the dancing, followed by the wedding party and guests. A reception custom with no religious content; couples who dread it can cut it without consequence.

customs.name: Bouquet toss
customs.description: The bride throws her bouquet over her shoulder to the unmarried guests; whoever catches it is said to marry next. Ask the florist for a small throwing copy if you want to keep the real one.

customs.name: The unity candle
customs.description: Two side candles lit by the mothers, from which the couple together light a central candle. A twentieth-century American custom, common at Methodist, Lutheran and Baptist weddings in the US, and rare in Britain. Where used it usually sits after the vows or rings; agree the placement with the minister.

customs.name: Communion at the wedding
customs.description: Anglican, Methodist and Lutheran services may include Holy Communion, turning the wedding into a full service of word and sacrament; Methodist practice invites the whole congregation to receive rather than the couple alone. Most couples keep the service without it, not least for length. Rare at Baptist weddings.

customs.name: A piper at Scottish weddings
customs.description: A bagpiper playing the couple out of the church and greeting guests at the reception is a fixture at many Scottish weddings, Church of Scotland included. Cultural rather than religious, and usually booked like any other musician.

gotchas: Talk to the church before you book anything else. The church's diary is set around Sunday services and other weddings, and in the Church of England the legal preliminaries hang off the church booking, not the other way round.

In the Church of England you cannot simply pick a pretty church. You must live in the parish or have a qualifying connection, such as baptism there, six months' past residence, six months on the worship register, or a parent or grandparent married in that church. Evidence is required, so start gathering it early.

Banns take real calendar time: three Sundays in the wedding church and in each parish where you live, and the wedding must happen within three months of the last reading. If you move house during the banns period, tell the vicar at once, because banns may need to be read again or replaced with a licence.

A Church of England wedding is legally binding in itself; the clergy handle registration and no registrar attends. Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian and Lutheran weddings in England and Wales instead need register office notice at least 29 days ahead, plus either the building's authorised person or a booked registrar. Couples who assume the chapel works like the parish church miss the notice deadline.
Register office notice names the exact building and is valid for twelve months. Change the venue and you must give notice, and pay, again.

If either of you is not a British or Irish citizen and lacks EU settled status, the banns route is not available: a Church of England wedding then needs a superintendent registrar's schedule, with notice published for 28 days and extendable to 70. Build that into the timeline, not the final month.

In England and Wales a wedding must take place between 8am and 6pm, and a minister cannot legally marry you outdoors, in a garden, marquee or hotel. Couples wanting an outdoor wedding usually have a civil ceremony and a separate church blessing. Scotland is the opposite: the law authorises the celebrant, not the building, so a Church of Scotland minister can marry you anywhere in Scotland he or she agrees to.

Marrying again after divorce is possible but discretionary almost everywhere. The Church of England has allowed it since 2002, yet each vicar decides, and some will offer a service of prayer and dedication after a civil wedding instead. Methodist and Church of Scotland ministers may remarry divorced people; Baptist practice varies congregation by congregation. Raise it at the very first meeting.

Same-sex marriage is not legally possible in the Church of England, though some parishes offer prayers of blessing. The Methodist Church of Great Britain has permitted same-sex marriage on registered premises since 2021, and several other denominations allow ministers or congregations to opt in, while many Baptist and conservative congregations do not. If this affects you, ask the individual church, because the denomination's headline position does not settle what your local minister will do.

Sunday weddings are rare in parish churches because the building and clergy are committed to services, and Saturday slots around other weddings and Saturday-evening obligations can pin your ceremony time. Confirm the time of day early, then build the reception around it.

Weddings in Lent are allowed in Protestant churches, but some keep the building undecorated or restrained in Lent and Advent, and at Christmas and Easter the flowers are already decided. Ask what the church will look like on your date before briefing a florist.

Music is more flexible than at a Catholic wedding, but it is still the vicar's or minister's call. Most are comfortable with the classic processionals and a mix of sacred and tasteful secular music; some churches, particularly Presbyterian ones in the US, require all music to be sacred and approved. Agree every piece before promising anything to a singer.
Filming the service usually raises the organist's and choir's fees because of performance rights. Tell the musicians the wedding will be filmed when you book, not when the videographer walks in.

Methodist premises are alcohol-free as a rule of the denomination, and many Baptist and other free-church halls are the same. If the reception is in a church hall, confirm the alcohol policy in writing before you plan a bar or buy wine.

In England and Wales you no longer get the marriage certificate on the day. You sign a schedule or marriage document in church, it goes back to the register office, and you order certificates afterwards; allow for that delay before honeymoon name changes. In Scotland the signed schedule must be returned to the registrar within three days, so appoint someone dependable.

US marriage licences have their own clock: many expire 30 to 90 days after issue and a few states impose a short waiting period. Getting the licence too early is as much a problem as too late, and the officiant, not you, must return it after the ceremony.
Many US pastors will not book a wedding without premarital counselling, often several sessions across a few months. Treat it as part of the timeline, not an optional extra to squeeze in at the end.

The church's optional extras are individually small and collectively real: organist, choir, bells, verger, heating, filming supplements and banns fees in a second parish. Ask for an itemised written quote at the start, which Church of England guidance itself recommends.
